lede: A body that is not accelerating has forces that cancel exactly. That single idea turns a picture of four forces into two ordinary equations, and those equations are where most of the marks in a Unit 2 forces question live.
can: Recognise when a body is in equilibrium and say what that means for its forces
Write two component equations, with every force in each of them
Find an unknown force or angle on the flat, on a slope and at a point

md: Stand still and two forces act on you: the Earth pulls you down, the floor pushes you up, and they match. Nothing is left over.

alt: A particle at O held still by three forces: 24 N horizontally to the right, 7 N vertically downwards, and 25 N up and to the left at 16.26 degrees to the horizontal.

caption: Three forces that add to nothing: 25 N up and to the left at 16.26° to the horizontal.

md: A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Not small: zero. So it stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line: nothing is left over to change its motion.

stem: The picture shows a particle held still by 24 N to the right, 7 N downwards and 25 N up and to the left at 16.26° to the horizontal. Check that nothing is left over.

steps.working: The 25 N splits: $25\cos 16.26° = 24$ N to the left and $25\sin 16.26° = 7$ N up
steps.decision: Only the angled force needs splitting; the other two already lie along the directions.
The part to the left matches the 24 N to the right.
The part upwards matches the 7 N downwards. Zero both ways: the resultant is zero.

prompt: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. What is the resultant of those forces?
options: zero
the largest of the three
the sum of the three sizes
explain: Equilibrium means the forces cancel in every direction, as steps 2 and 3 of See it showed across and up: nothing is left over, so the resultant is zero. Anything left over would accelerate the particle.

twin.prompt: A ring is held still by four strings pulling in different directions. Which must be true?
options: The forces on it cancel in every direction
The four tensions are equal
The largest tension equals the total of the other three
twin.answer: The forces on it cancel in every direction
twin.explain: Held still means no acceleration, so the four pulls cancel in every direction and nothing is left over.

optionNotes.option: The four tensions are equal
optionNotes.why: Strings pulling in different directions can balance with different sizes; nothing makes them equal.

optionNotes.option: The largest tension equals the total of the other three
optionNotes.why: That adds sizes as if every string pulled along one line. They pull in different directions, so it is their parts that cancel.

optionNotes.option: the largest of the three
optionNotes.why: No single force survives: every force takes part in the balance, so nothing at all is left over.

optionNotes.option: the sum of the three sizes
optionNotes.why: Adding sizes ignores the directions, and it is the directions that make the forces cancel.

md: A zero resultant means zero in every direction, so choose two perpendicular ones and write an equation for each: horizontal and vertical on the flat, along and across a slope. Two equations find two unknowns.

title: Why two directions are enough
md: Any force can be rebuilt from its parts along two perpendicular directions, so if both totals are zero nothing is left in any direction. A third equation would only repeat the first two.

stem: A rope pulls a box of weight 50 N with a force of 20 N at 30° above the horizontal, and the box does not move. Find the normal reaction.

steps.decision: One resolved component: the start of the method, worth a method mark at most.
The marks that follow belong to the equation with every vertical force in it.
Only the complete equation gives the value.

prompt: A candidate resolves one force on a body in equilibrium and writes down its vertical component, then stops. What is missing?
options: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
the horizontal component of that same force
the mass of the body
answer: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
explain: A single component is where the method starts, as step 1 of See it showed; the marks that follow are for the equation with every vertical force in it, set equal to zero.

twin.prompt: A candidate on a slope question writes $30\cos 20°$ for one force's component and stops. What is still missing?
options: an equation with every force in that direction, set to zero
the other component of the same force
the angle of the slope
twin.answer: an equation with every force in that direction, set to zero
twin.explain: The component goes into an equation with every force in that direction; the marks are for that equation.

optionNotes.option: the other component of the same force
optionNotes.why: That belongs to the other direction's equation; this direction still has no equation at all.

optionNotes.option: the angle of the slope
optionNotes.why: The angle is already inside the component. What is missing is the equation the component belongs in.

optionNotes.option: the horizontal component of that same force
optionNotes.why: The other component belongs to the other equation. What earns the marks here is this direction's equation, with every vertical force in it.

optionNotes.option: the mass of the body
optionNotes.why: The weight may well be needed, but as one term of the equation; the equation itself is what is missing.

text: Where the two equations come from

md: Add up the horizontal parts of all the forces to get $X$, and the vertical parts to get $Y$. The resultant is the diagonal of the rectangle they make, so by Pythagoras its size is $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$. That is zero only when $X = 0$ and $Y = 0$ together: which is exactly the pair of equations.

stem: Show that the resultant of a set of forces is zero exactly when the horizontal parts total zero and the vertical parts total zero.

steps.working: Horizontal parts total $X$; vertical parts total $Y$
steps.decision: Every force splits into a horizontal and a vertical part; add each set.
The totals are at right angles, so the resultant is the diagonal of their rectangle, by Pythagoras.
A sum of two squares is zero only when both squares are.

steps.working: For example, $X = 6$ and $Y = 8$ give $\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$ N: not equilibrium
steps.decision: One total at zero is not enough; both must be.

prompt: The horizontal parts of the forces on a particle add to 0 N and the vertical parts add to 12 N upwards. What is the size of the resultant, in newtons?
explain: The resultant has size $\sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, as step 2 of See it showed. Here $X = 0$ and $Y = 12$, so it is $\sqrt{0 + 144} = 12$ N: one equation holding is not enough, both must.

twin.prompt: The horizontal parts of the forces on a particle add to 5 N and the vertical parts add to 12 N. What is the size of the resultant, in newtons?

md: The commonest way marks go is an equation with too few terms. A rope at an angle has a part that lifts, so the vertical equation holds three forces: the reaction, the rope's lift and the weight.

title: What the reports keep saying
md: Equations with only two terms are described as very common, and a large number of candidates never set up the vertical equation at all. Both lose the marks that the equation itself carries.

stem: A 12 kg block rests on a rough table while a rope pulls it with 45 N at 35° above the table, and it does not move. Find the normal reaction and the friction. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: The mass becomes a force before it goes into an equation: 12 kg weighs 120 N.
Three forces have vertical parts: the reaction, the rope's lift and the weight.
The rope lifts part of the weight, so the table holds less than all of it.
The block does not move, so friction matches the rope's pull along the table.

prompt: A block of weight 60 N rests on a table and a rope pulls it with a vertical component of 24 N upwards. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
explain: Three forces have vertical parts, as in step 2 of See it: the reaction and the rope's 24 N together hold up the 60 N weight. Resolving vertically, $R + 24 = 60$, so $R = 36$ N.

twin.prompt: A block of weight 85 N rests on a table and a rope pulls it with a vertical component of 31 N upwards. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?

text: Smooth slope: a rope holds it

alt: A box of mass 18 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 24 degrees by a rope along the slope: T up the slope, R at right angles to it, and 180 N straight down.

md: On a slope the useful pair of directions is along the surface and at right angles to it, because two of the three forces already lie along them. Only the weight has to be resolved.
Check the answers by size: the reaction and the tension each come out smaller than the weight, since each balances only a part of it. A swapped sine and cosine usually shows up here.

stem: An 18 kg box is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 24° by a rope along the slope. Find the tension and the normal reaction. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: Only the weight has to be split; the tension and the reaction already lie along the two directions.
Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle, so it takes the sine.
Into the slope is beside the angle, so it takes the cosine; less than the weight, as it must be.

prompt: A box is held at rest on a smooth slope by a rope parallel to the slope. How does the normal reaction on it compare with its weight?
options: it is smaller than the weight
it is equal to the weight
it is larger than the weight
answer: it is smaller than the weight
explain: Only the part of the weight pressing into the slope has to be balanced, $mg\cos\alpha$, as step 3 of See it showed; $\cos\alpha$ is less than one on any real slope, so the reaction is smaller than the weight.

twin.prompt: A crate is held at rest on a smooth slope by a rope parallel to the slope. The slope is made steeper. What happens to the normal reaction?
options: it gets smaller
it stays equal to the weight
it gets larger
twin.explain: A steeper slope has a larger angle and a smaller cosine, so less of the weight presses into it.

optionNotes.option: it stays equal to the weight
optionNotes.why: On any slope the reaction balances only mg cos α, which is less than the weight.

optionNotes.option: it gets larger
optionNotes.why: Steeper means a larger angle and a smaller cosine, so less of the weight presses into the slope.

optionNotes.option: it is equal to the weight
optionNotes.why: That is true only on a level surface. On a slope only the part of the weight pressing in, mg cos α, is balanced.

optionNotes.option: it is larger than the weight
optionNotes.why: No part of a force is bigger than the force itself: cos α is less than one, so the reaction is smaller.

text: On a rough slope: friction holds it

caption: No rope: friction up the slope is what holds it.

md: Take the rope away and a box on a rough slope can still sit there. Friction has taken the rope's place, so it acts up the slope and matches the part of the weight pulling the box down it.

stem: A 7 kg crate rests on a rough slope inclined at 18° with nothing attached. Find the friction and the normal reaction. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.working: Along the slope: $F = 70\sin 18° = 21.63$ N, up the slope
steps.decision: Friction is the only force along the surface, so it matches the weight's part down the slope.
The reaction balances the part pressing in.

prompt: A crate rests on a rough slope with nothing attached to it. Which force balances the component of the weight acting down the slope?
options: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
the normal reaction
the whole weight
answer: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it can do nothing along it; friction is the only force left along the surface, and it acts up the slope, as step 1 of See it showed.

twin.prompt: A box rests on a rough slope with nothing attached. Which force balances the component of the weight pressing into the slope?
options: the normal reaction
the force due to friction
the whole weight
twin.explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, the same line as the part of the weight pressing in, so it balances that part.

optionNotes.option: the force due to friction
optionNotes.why: Friction lies along the slope, so it has no part pressing into it; it balances the part down the slope.

optionNotes.option: the whole weight
optionNotes.why: Only a part of the weight presses into the slope, and a force cannot balance itself.

optionNotes.option: the normal reaction
optionNotes.why: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it has no part along it: it balances the part pressing in instead.

optionNotes.option: the whole weight
optionNotes.why: The whole weight is not along the slope; only its part down the slope needs balancing.

text: At a point: two equations, two unknowns

md: When an unknown force P acts at an unknown angle θ, write its two parts as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ and let the two equations find them. The papers set this shape at a point with three or four forces.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Lami's theorem, the triangle of forces and friction as $F = \mu R$ are A-level methods. CCEA's equilibrium questions are solved with two component equations, and friction is given or found from the balance.

stem: A particle is held in equilibrium by 21 N to the right, 20 N downwards and a force $P$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, to the left. Find $P$ and $\theta$.

steps.decision: The unknown force's two parts balance the other two forces.
Two equations, two unknowns.
$P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with longest side $P$.
Dividing removes $P$ and leaves the angle.

title: FM Mechanics resolving around a point
why: Taught straight against this specification. Watch the two directions being named in writing before either equation is formed.

prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 9 N to the right, 12 N downwards and a force P at an angle θ above the horizontal, to the left. Which pair of equations is right?
options: P cos θ = 9 and P sin θ = 12
P sin θ = 9 and P cos θ = 12
answer: P cos θ = 9 and P sin θ = 12
explain: The angle is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal part of P takes the cosine and balances the 9 N, and the vertical part takes the sine and balances the 12 N, as in steps 1 and 2 of See it.

twin.prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 16 N to the left, 30 N upwards and a force Q at an angle α below the horizontal, to the right. Which pair of equations is right?
options: Q cos α = 16 and Q sin α = 30
Q sin α = 16 and Q cos α = 30
twin.answer: Q cos α = 16 and Q sin α = 30
twin.explain: Measured from the horizontal, the horizontal part takes the cosine and balances the 16 N; the vertical part takes the sine and balances the 30 N.

optionNotes.option: Q sin α = 16 and Q cos α = 30
optionNotes.why: Measured from the horizontal, the horizontal part takes the cosine, not the sine.
Forces at right angles do not add as sizes; Q's two parts balance the 16 N and the 30 N separately.

optionNotes.option: P sin θ = 9 and P cos θ = 12
optionNotes.why: The angle is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal part is next to it and takes the cosine.
The 9 N and 12 N are at right angles, so their sizes do not add; P's two parts balance them separately.

prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 9 N to the right, 12 N downwards and a third force. What is the magnitude of the third force, in newtons?
explain: The third force's parts balance the other two, so they are 9 N and 12 N: the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle, as in step 3 of See it. $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15$ N.

twin.prompt: A particle is held in equilibrium by 16 N to the left, 30 N upwards and a third force. What is the magnitude of the third force, in newtons?

md: Equilibrium does not mean stationary. A body moving at constant velocity is not accelerating, so $F = ma$ gives a resultant of zero and the forces balance exactly as they do at rest. *At rest*, *held still* and *moving with constant velocity* are one instruction.
A pull at an angle both drags and lifts: its part along the ground meets the friction, and its part upwards takes some of the weight off the ground.

stem: A 5 kg sledge is dragged at a constant velocity by a rope pulling 44 N at 20° above the ground. Find the friction and the normal reaction. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: Constant velocity, so no acceleration: friction matches the pull's part along the ground.
The rope lifts part of the 50 N weight.

prompt: A crate is being dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of 2 m/s. What is true of the forces on it?
options: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
they do not balance, because it is moving
the driving force must be the largest
answer: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
explain: Constant velocity means the speed is not changing, so a = 0 and F = ma makes the resultant zero, as in step 1 of See it, where the friction matched the pull's part along the ground exactly.

twin.prompt: A parachutist falls at a steady 5 m/s. How does the air resistance on her compare with her weight?
options: it is equal to her weight
it is smaller than her weight
it is larger than her weight
twin.answer: it is equal to her weight
twin.explain: A steady speed means no acceleration, so the two forces balance exactly.

optionNotes.option: it is smaller than her weight
optionNotes.why: Then a downward resultant would be left over and she would speed up.

optionNotes.option: it is larger than her weight
optionNotes.why: Then she would slow down. A steady speed means the two forces match.

optionNotes.option: they do not balance, because it is moving
optionNotes.why: Moving is not accelerating: at a steady velocity nothing is left over, so the forces balance.

optionNotes.option: the driving force must be the largest
optionNotes.why: A larger driving force would leave a resultant and speed the crate up; at a constant velocity pull and friction match.

md: **An angle to the vertical** (2024, 2026). A force is given at an angle to the vertical, not the horizontal. First line: its vertical part now takes the cosine and its horizontal part the sine.
**Mark the forces** (2019). A part asks you to mark the forces on the diagram before any equation. First line: each force with an arrow and a label, the weight included.
**One way still, the other moving** (2019, 2023). A block pulled at an angle is in equilibrium vertically, which gives the reaction, while along the floor $F = ma$.
**A steady speed** (2023). Moving at constant velocity is equilibrium too, so the forces along the floor balance and friction is the pull's part along it.

stem: A force of 40 N acts at 20° to the vertical. Find its vertical and horizontal parts.

steps.decision: Measured from the vertical, the side next to the angle is the vertical one, so it takes the cosine.
The side opposite the angle is the horizontal one, so it takes the sine.

prompt: A force of 30 N acts at 50° to the vertical. Which expression gives its horizontal part?
explain: Measured from the vertical, the side next to the angle is the vertical part, so the vertical part takes the cosine and the horizontal part the sine, as step 2 of See it showed: $30\sin 50°$.

twin.prompt: A force of 18 N acts at 25° to the vertical. Which expression gives its vertical part?
twin.explain: From the vertical, the vertical side is next to the angle, so it takes the cosine.

optionNotes.why: From the vertical, the sine gives the horizontal part, the side opposite the angle.
The tangent compares the two parts; it never gives either of them from the force.
From the vertical, the cosine gives the vertical part; the horizontal side is opposite the angle and takes the sine.
The tangent compares the two parts with each other; it never gives a part of the force.

text: See it: still one way, moving the other

stem: A 10 kg block is pulled along a smooth floor by a rope at 30° above the floor with a force of 40 N. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

steps.decision: The block neither rises nor sinks, so the vertical forces balance.

steps.working: Along the floor, not in equilibrium: $40\cos 30° = 10a$, so $a = 3.46$ m/s²
steps.decision: Nothing opposes the pull's part along the smooth floor, so it accelerates the block.

prompt: A block is pulled along a smooth floor by a rope at an angle. Part (i) asks for the normal reaction and part (ii) for the acceleration. Which part uses equilibrium?
options: Part (i): vertically nothing accelerates
Part (ii): the block moves along the floor
Neither part
explain: The block does not rise or sink, so vertically the forces balance and give the reaction, as step 1 of See it did; along the floor it speeds up, so part (ii) uses F = ma.

twin.prompt: A sledge is pulled across smooth ice by a rope at an angle, and it speeds up. Which equation uses equilibrium?
options: The vertical one, for the normal reaction
The horizontal one, for the acceleration
Both of them
twin.answer: The vertical one, for the normal reaction
twin.explain: Vertically nothing accelerates, so that equation balances; along the ice the sledge speeds up, so that one is F = ma.

optionNotes.option: The horizontal one, for the acceleration
optionNotes.why: The sledge speeds up along the ice, so that equation is F = ma, not a balance.

optionNotes.option: Both of them
optionNotes.why: Only the vertical direction balances; along the ice there is a resultant, which is why it speeds up.

optionNotes.option: Part (ii): the block moves along the floor
optionNotes.why: Along the floor the block speeds up, so that part uses F = ma, not a balance.

optionNotes.option: Neither part
optionNotes.why: The block neither rises nor sinks, so vertically nothing accelerates: part (i) is an equilibrium even though the block moves.

caption: Two unknowns, one along each direction, and angles to both lines.

md: The hardest shape so far (2024, 2026) puts four forces at a point: one unknown horizontal, one unknown vertical, and two known forces at angles, one to the vertical and one to the horizontal.

stem: Four forces hold a point in equilibrium: 30 N at 35° to the vertical (up and to the right), 16 N at 25° below the horizontal (to the right), $P$ N horizontally to the left and $W$ N vertically downwards. Find $W$ and $P$.

steps.decision: The 35° is from the vertical, so its vertical part takes the cosine; the 25° is from the horizontal, so its vertical part takes the sine.
Both angled forces push to the right, so their horizontal parts add; P alone balances them.

prompt: Four forces hold a point still: an unknown P horizontal, an unknown W vertical and two known forces at angles. Why can each unknown be found from one equation?
options: Each unknown lies along one of the two directions, so it appears in one equation only
The two known forces cancel each other
W is always the largest force
answer: Each unknown lies along one of the two directions, so it appears in one equation only
explain: P is horizontal, so it has no vertical part, and W is vertical, so it has no horizontal part; each equation holds just one unknown, as steps 1 and 2 of See it showed.

twin.prompt: Four forces hold a point still: an unknown horizontal force, an unknown vertical force and two known forces at angles. Which equation gives the unknown horizontal force?
options: Resolving horizontally
Resolving vertically
Pythagoras on the two known forces
twin.explain: The unknown horizontal force has no vertical part, so it appears only in the horizontal equation.

optionNotes.option: Resolving vertically
optionNotes.why: A horizontal force has no vertical part, so it cannot appear in the vertical equation.

optionNotes.option: Pythagoras on the two known forces
optionNotes.why: Pythagoras combines two parts at right angles; here each unknown sits alone in one resolved equation.

optionNotes.option: The two known forces cancel each other
optionNotes.why: They have different sizes and angles; their parts appear in both equations rather than cancelling.

optionNotes.option: W is always the largest force
optionNotes.why: Size has nothing to do with it: W appears in one equation only because it has no horizontal part.

md:
Say what equilibrium means, and read at rest, held still and constant velocity as one instruction.
Write a complete equation in each of two perpendicular directions, every force included.
Resolve along and across a slope, with friction holding a body still on a rough one.
Find an unknown force and angle at a point, with angles to either line.
Spot the twists: the diagram, still one way and moving the other, a steady speed.

An equilibrium part is worth 2 or 3 marks and is worded 'Calculate the value of' or 'Calculate the normal reaction'. The first mark is for naming the direction you are resolving in and writing a complete equation; the last is for the value to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Write 'resolving vertically' on its own line, then list every force that has a vertical part.
